marble.name: Vibrations & Sound
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Understand that vibrating materials can make sound, and that sound can make materials vibrate
marble.prompt: Can you pluck a rubber band and explain that the vibrating band makes the sound, and then hold a ruler on a speaker and see it shake from the music?

cluster.summary: Your child is investigating light and sound — discovering how we see objects, experimenting with transparent and opaque materials, and learning how vibrations create sound.

misconceptions: Only things you can SEE vibrating make sound; where no vibration is visible the sound must come from something else (usually 'because you hit it / blew it').
Sound is a kind of substance or particle, and different sounds are made of different kinds of stuff.
A sound is explained by the material ('it's metal') rather than by the act of vibrating.
Vibration makes sound, but sound cannot make things vibrate (missing the reverse direction).
Sound travels only in a straight line to the listener's ear, rather than spreading out (a foundation-stage seed of a later misconception).
representations: Rice, salt or a light ball bouncing on a drum skin (vibration made visible)
A tuning fork — dipped in water (splashes), touched to the cheek (felt), held against a table (heard louder)
A plucked stretched elastic band or guitar string blurring into visible to-and-fro
Finger on the throat / larynx while humming or speaking
Paper or a light flag fluttering in front of a speaker (sound → vibration direction)
authoredAnswer: The block IS vibrating — moving back and forth very fast, too small to see — and that vibration is what makes the sound. We could check by touching it to feel the buzz, or by resting light grains on it (or dipping it in water) to reveal the wobble.
probe: Rest a few grains of rice on a drum skin. Predict what will happen to the rice when you bang the drum (or shout right next to it) — and say why before you try. Then do it and explain what it shows about vibration and sound.

wrongAnswers.wrong: There's no vibration — the sound just comes from hitting the block hard.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Denies vibration in a struck block, clinked stones, or a wind instrument; credits the human action instead
wrongAnswers.fix: Run a recurring 'spot the vibration' routine; make invisible vibrations visible or felt (rice on a drum, tuning fork dipped in water, fingers on the throat); deliberately choose non-obvious sound sources.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Talks about sound as a material emitted and travelling out, rather than as a vibration passed on
wrongAnswers.fix: Reframe sound as a vibration that is passed along, not matter that leaves the object; nothing is 'used up' or emitted as a substance.

wrongAnswers.wrong: Only vibrating things make sound; a sound can't make anything else vibrate.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Accepts vibration-to-sound but denies sound-to-vibration (e.g. doubts that rice will jump when you shout near a drum)
wrongAnswers.fix: Rice-on-a-drum or a paper flag on a speaker cone — sound carries energy that shakes things; the link runs both ways.
